Zora Neale Hurston. The novelist, folklorist, and anthropologist who celebrated Black Southern vernacular culture and folk traditions at a time when such material was often denigrated. Her novel Their Eyes Were Watching God stands as a modernist masterpiece centering a Black woman's voice, agency, and self-discovery.

Their Eyes Were Watching God uses stream-of-consciousness narration and Black vernacular speech to tell the story of Janie Crawford's three marriages and her journey toward autonomy and self-understanding. Hurston was trained as an anthropologist, and she collected African-American folklore, folk songs, and oral traditions in the South and Caribbean, bringing scholarly rigor to material often dismissed by the academy. Her use of dialect and vernacular was politically charged—she celebrated Black speech as literary-worthy rather than apologizing for it or erasing it.

Beyond her major novel, Hurston wrote short stories, essays, and plays exploring themes of love, independence, community, and the spiritual dimensions of Black life. Later in her life, she faced relative obscurity and poverty, partly because her lyrical, folk-centered work was eclipsed by the protest literature of the nineteen-forties and fifties. But her reputation was revived by feminist and Black literary scholars in the nineteen-seventies and eighties, restoring her as a crucial figure in American modernism. Her legacy influenced both Gwendolyn Brooks, the poet who later also centered Black women's inner lives and agency, and Alice Walker, who wrote Hurston's biography and championed her legacy throughout her own career.
